import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 945

*References:*
 - [erdosproblems.com/945](https://www.erdosproblems.com/945)
 - [ErMi52] Erdős, P. and Mirsky, L., The distribution of values of the divisor function {$d(n)$}. Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) (1952), 257--271.
-/

open Filter Real

namespace Erdos945

abbrev τ  := fun (n : ℕ) => n.divisors.card

/--
Let $F(x)$ be the maximal $k$ such that there exist $n+1, \dots, n+k \le x$
with $τ(n+1), \dots, τ(n+k)$ all distinct, where $τ(m)$ counts the divisors of $m$. -/
noncomputable def F (x : ℝ) : ℕ :=
  sSup {k | ∃ (n : ℕ), n + k ≤ x ∧ (Set.Ioc n (n + k)).InjOn τ}

-- Implementation note: we define a Prop here and below to be able to easily formulate
-- the equivalence between the two variants. Because the theorems require `answer(sorry)` we
-- can't handle this with `type_of%`.
def Erdos945Prop : Prop := ∃ O : ℝ → ℝ, O =O[atTop] (1 : ℝ → ℝ) ∧ ∀ᶠ x in atTop, F x ≤ log x ^ O x

/--
Is it true that $F(x) \leq (\log x)^{O(1)}$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_945 : answer(sorry) ↔ Erdos945Prop := by
  sorry

def Erdos945Constant : Prop :=
  ∃ C > (0 : ℝ),  ∀ᶠ x : ℝ in atTop,
    ∃ a b : ℕ, a ≠ b ∧
    ↑a ∈ Set.Icc x (x + log x ^ C) ∧
    ↑b ∈ Set.Icc x (x + log x ^ C) ∧
    τ a = τ b

/--
Is there a constant $C > 0$ such that, for all large $x$, every interval $[x, x+(\log x)C]$
contains two integers with the same number of divisors?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_945.variants.constant : answer(sorry) ↔ Erdos945Constant := by
  sorry

-- TODO(firsching): show equivalence
/--
The two ways of phrasing the conjecture are equivalent.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_945.variants.equivalence : Erdos945Prop ↔ Erdos945Constant := by
  sorry

/--
Erdős and Mirsky [ErMi52] proved that $\frac{(\log x)^{1/2}}{\log\log x}\ll F(x)$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_945.variants.lower_bound :
    (fun (x : ℕ) => (log x).sqrt /(log x).log) =O[atTop] fun (n : ℕ) => (F n : ℝ) := by
  sorry

/--
Erdős and Mirsky [ErMi52] proved that $\log F(x) \ll \frac{(\log x)^{1/2}}$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_945.variants.upper_bound :
    (fun (n : ℕ) => (F n : ℝ).log) =O[atTop] fun (x : ℕ) => (log x).sqrt /(log x).log := by
  sorry

-- TODO(firsching): add observations what follows from Cramér's conjecture and if every sufficient
-- interval contains a squarefree number.

end Erdos945

findings.description: The docstring at line 58 gives the interval `[x, x+(\log x)C]`, which denotes length C·log x rather than (log x)^C. The Lean predicate correctly uses `log x ^ C`; only the mathematical prose is wrong.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/945 asks whether some C > 0 makes every interval [x, x+(log x)^C] contain two distinct integers with the same divisor count, for all sufficiently large x.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring interval to `$[x, x+(\log x)^C]$`. Leave the Lean statement unchanged.

findings.description: The docstring at line 82 contains the unfinished fraction `\frac{(\log x)^{1/2}}`, omitting the log log x denominator. The Lean statement includes that denominator and correctly matches the cited result. Removing the denominator from the Lean formula would not be the appropriate repair.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/945 records the Erdős–Mirsky bound F(x) ≪ exp(O(sqrt(log x)/log log x)). Erdős and Mirsky, The distribution of values of the divisor function d(n), Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) 2 (1952), p. 258, likewise give F(x) < exp(c₃ sqrt(log x)/log log x): https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1952-12.pdf.
findings.suggested_fix: Complete the docstring formula as `$\log F(x) \ll \frac{(\log x)^{1/2}}{\log\log x}$`. Leave the Lean statement unchanged.

reformulations.difference: The polylogarithmic bound is encoded using an x-dependent, possibly negative real exponent O(x) satisfying O =O[atTop] 1, rather than explicitly choosing one positive constant exponent.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: This is equivalent to ∃ C > 0, eventually F(x) ≤ (log x)^C. Big-O supplies a positive constant C with |O(x)| ≤ C eventually. Once log x ≥ 1, monotonicity in the exponent gives (log x)^O(x) ≤ (log x)^C. Conversely, the constant function O(x)=C is O(1). This exact equivalence was proved independently in /workspace/review/checks.lean.

reformulations.difference: The source uses the real parameter x, whereas the Lean asymptotic lower bound is restricted to natural-number arguments.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For x ≥ 0, F(x)=F(floor x), proved independently in Lean. Put h(x)=sqrt(log x)/log log x. For sufficiently large n and n ≤ x < n+1, h(n)/2 ≤ h(x) ≤ 2h(n), by comparing log x with log n and log log x with log log n. Thus h(n)=O(F(n)) on naturals extends to h(x)=O(F(x)) on reals; the converse follows by restriction. The full asymptotic equivalence was checked mathematically, not proved in Lean.

reformulations.difference: The source's exponential upper bound for F(x) is stated as a Big-O bound on log(F(n)), and only at natural-number arguments.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Let h(x)=sqrt(log x)/log log x. Eventually F(x) ≥ 1 and h(x)>0, with h(x) tending to infinity. Taking logarithms converts F(x) ≤ A·exp(Bh(x)) into log F(x) ≤ log A+Bh(x); the additive constant is absorbed into O(h(x)). Conversely, exponentiation gives the source bound. Natural and real arguments are interchangeable because F(x)=F(floor x) and h(x) is within fixed positive factors of h(floor x) for large x.

review.notes: No substantive misformalizations or status discrepancies were found; both findings are documentation-only. The current source still marks the problem OPEN. Its newer upper-bound improvement does not invalidate the historically attributed theorem. The interval equivalence is sound: increasing the exponent absorbs integer rounding and fixed initial segments. Independent scratch proofs establish boundedness and attainment of F's supremum, F(x)=F(floor x) for x≥0, and equality with a computable finite search. That search was evaluated through 30, with small cases also proved by decide. These checks have no sorryAx dependency. Zero-divisor and logarithm default values do not affect the asymptotic claims. No repository files were changed by this review.
